rules.rule:
PRE-STAGE (whitespace normalization, applies to everything below): before any parsing, the source has U+0002 (STX) and U+0003 (ETX) characters deleted, "
" and lone "" replaced by "
", then "

ENTITY PRE-STAGE (numeric character references are normalized by the HTML-extraction preprocessor, i.e. BEFORE block parsing and BEFORE inline parsing, so it also rewrites text inside code spans and code blocks). Scan the whole normalized document left to right. When an '&' is found: (A) if the next char is '#', try to match, anchored at the '&', the regex `&#(?:[0-9]+|[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+)[^0-9a-fA-F]` (note: greedy digit run, and one MANDATORY trailing character that is NOT a hex digit [0-9a-fA-F]; standard regex backtracking applies). If it matches with total length L, let name = source[i+2 .. i+L-2] (the match minus the leading '&#' and minus its final terminator char); emit the text `&` + `#` + name + `;`; then set k = i+L, and if source[k-1] != ';' set k = k-1; continue scanning at k. If it does NOT match, emit the two literal characters `&#` and continue scanning at i+2. (B) if the next char is not '#', try to match `&([a-zA-Z][-.a-zA-Z0-9]*);` anchored at the '&'; if it matches, emit the matched text verbatim (identity — no observable change) and continue after it; otherwise emit a literal `&` and continue at i+1. Nothing is ever dropped and parsing never aborts.

The entity pre-stage rewrite is observable inside code spans and indented code blocks (proving it happens before block/inline parsing), but NOT inside raw HTML tags (whose text is consumed wholesale by the HTML extractor).

The entity pre-stage never disables later parsing: an unresolvable '&' (e.g. `&nbsp` with no semicolon, or `&#x;`) does not prevent subsequent inline HTML, block-level HTML, or HTML comments from being recognized.

SERIALIZER TEXT ESCAPING (applies to every text/tail string in the element tree, in this order): (1) replace each '&' that is NOT immediately followed by a valid entity reference body with `&` — 'valid' means the regex `&(?:\#[0-9]+|\#[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+|[a-zA-Z0-9]+);` matches starting at that '&'; (2) replace '<' with `<`; (3) replace '>' with `>`. Double quote and single quote are NEVER escaped in text.

SERIALIZER ATTRIBUTE ESCAPING (applies to every attribute value, in this order): (1) same conditional '&' rule as text (escape '&' to `&` only when it does not start a valid entity reference per `&(?:\#[0-9]+|\#[xX][0-9a-fA-F]+|[a-zA-Z0-9]+);`); (2) '<' -> `<`; (3) '>' -> `>`; (4) '"' -> `"`. Single quote is NOT escaped.

Text placed in an 'atomic' (no-further-inline-processing) node, such as autolink link text, is subject only to the serializer's conditional text escaping — a literal `&` there stays `&` (NOT `&amp;`), while a bare `&` becomes `&`.
Text inside stashed raw HTML (block-level HTML, raw tags, comments) bypasses ALL escaping and is emitted byte-for-byte.

INLINE PATTERN PRIORITY (highest first, all relevant to this area): backtick/code-span (190) > backslash-escape (180) > reference (170) > link (160) > image_link (150) > image_reference (140) > short_reference (130) > short_image_ref (125) > autolink (120) > automail (110) > linebreak (100) > raw-inline-html (90) > entity (80) > not_strong (70) > em_strong (60/50). Each pattern is applied repeatedly (one match at a time) over the whole buffer until it no longer matches, before the next-lower pattern is tried. Consequence: code spans are found before escapes, links, and raw inline HTML.

CODE SPAN MATCHING ALGORITHM. Over the current inline buffer, for i = 0,1,2,... try in order: (ALT-1) if (i == 0 or buf[i-1] != '\\') and buf[i] == '\\': let B = length of the run of consecutive backslashes starting at i; if B is even and buf[i+B] == '`', then this is a match that consumes exactly those B backslashes and produces B/2 literal backslash characters (protected from further processing); restart the scan at index 0. If neither alternative matches, advance i by 1. The newline character IS matchable by the content, so code spans may span multiple lines of the same block.

A run of two or more backticks with nothing between them, or with only whitespace between them, still forms a span; if the stripped content is empty the result is ``. A single lone pair of backticks with nothing at all between them (``) is NOT a span because the content must be at least one character.

The block parser runs BEFORE inline processing.

A code span opener is suppressed when the character immediately before the first backtick is a single backslash (odd-length backslash run). With an EVEN-length backslash run immediately before the backticks, ALT-1 fires first: the run is consumed and replaced by half as many literal backslashes, and the span still forms afterwards.
A backslash inside a code span's content does NOT escape the closing backtick — the closing-run search ignores backslashes entirely.

BACKSLASH ESCAPE PATTERN: match `\` followed by any single character (INCLUDING a newline). The exactly-16 escapable characters are: \ ` * _ { } [ ] ( ) > # + - . !  (backslash, backtick, asterisk, underscore, open/close brace, open/close bracket, open/close paren, greater-than, hash, plus, hyphen, period, exclamation). If the following character is one of these, the two-character sequence is replaced by that single character, protected from all further inline processing (but still subject to serializer escaping at the end). NOTE: '<' is NOT escapable.

If the character after the backslash is NOT one of the 16 escapable characters, BOTH characters are left in the text verbatim (the backslash is kept), and the escape scanner resumes AFTER both characters (so that second character can never be re-used as the start of a new escape). Non-escapable includes: < | : " ' & ~ ^ = , / ; ? @ $ % digits letters space tab newline and all non-ASCII.

A backslash immediately followed by a newline is NOT a hard line break: both the backslash and the newline are kept verbatim (a hard break requires two-or-more spaces before the newline, of which exactly the last two are consumed). A backslash at the very end of the document is emitted as a literal backslash.

Backslash sequences are consumed left-to-right in non-overlapping pairs: an even-length run of backslashes yields half as many literal backslashes; with an odd-length run the trailing backslash escapes the character after it (if escapable) or is kept literally with it.

Escaped characters are protected only from INLINE pattern matching, not from serializer escaping: the only escapable character affected is '>', which comes back out as `>` in text and as `>` in attribute values.
Escapes are unescaped inside attribute values too (URLs, titles, alt text), and inside autolink hrefs/text.

When an escaped character ends up inside text that the raw-inline-HTML pattern later matches, the BACKSLASH IS RESTORED (the stashed raw HTML gets `\` + char, not just char). So `<b title="\*x">` is emitted with the backslash intact.

Escapes are inline-level and cannot prevent a block construct by 'escaping the marker'; they work only incidentally because a line starting with `\` no longer starts with the block marker character. Escaping the digit of an ordered list marker does nothing (digits are not escapable), but escaping the '.' does.
Escaping '!' and '[' suppresses image/link syntax; escaping only '!' still leaves the link.

Because code spans are matched before every other inline pattern, a code span at the very start or the very end of a paragraph, or occupying the whole paragraph, behaves identically; and code spans nest inside emphasis/links (as children) but emphasis/links never form inside a code span.

A hard line break (` \n` -> `
\n`) is not produced inside a code span, and trailing spaces at the very end of a paragraph (with no following line) are preserved verbatim in the output.

result.area: emphasis / strong emphasis (`*` and `_`), Python-Markdown 3.10.2 "smart emphasis" default

rules.rule: PIPELINE POSITION AND ORDER. Emphasis is produced by THREE separate inline patterns that run as three independent, sequential passes over the block's text. The full inline registry (priority, highest first) is: backtick(190), escape(180), reference(170), link(160), image_link(150), image_reference(140), short_reference(130), short_image_ref(125), autolink(120), automail(110), linebreak(100), html(90), entity(80), not_strong(70), em_strong(60 = asterisk processor, trigger regex `\*`), em_strong2(50 = underscore processor, trigger regex `_`). Each pattern is run to exhaustion over the whole text BEFORE the next pattern starts. Consequence: every `*` span in the text is resolved before any `_` span is even looked at, so a `*` span may steal a `_` opener/closer and vice versa never happens.

PER-PASS SCAN LOOP. For a pattern P with trigger regex T: set i=0; find successive non-overlapping matches of T in the text starting at i (left to right). For each such match at position p, call handleMatch at p. The FIRST p at which handleMatch succeeds wins: the text slice [start,end) that handleMatch reports is replaced by a placeholder string `klzzwxh:NNNN` (NNNN = zero-padded-to-4 decimal index into a global stash, starting at 0000 and incrementing for every stashed node in the whole document block), and the scan for P RESTARTS at index 0 of the NEW text. Repeat until no trigger position yields a success, then move on to the next pattern. Placeholders are opaque to later passes: they contain no `*` and no `_`, their first char is U+0002 (STX) and last char is U+0003 (ETX), and neither STX nor ETX is a `\w` char or a `\s` char. Therefore a stashed span is transparent to `[^\*]+` / `[^*]+` / `(.+?)` and it never blocks a `(?<!\w)` / `(?!\w)` guard.

not_strong PASS (priority 70, runs BEFORE both emphasis passes). Regex NOT_STRONG_RE = `((^|(?<=\s))(\*{1,3}|_{1,3})(?=\s|$))`, compiled with re.DOTALL|re.UNICODE (NOT re.MULTILINE). It matches a run of 1, 2 or 3 `*`, or 1, 2 or 3 `_`, such that: (a) the run starts at index 0 of the text, or the character immediately before it is a `\s` char; AND (b) the character immediately after the run is a `\s` char, or the run ends at end-of-text (`$` = end of text, or immediately before a single trailing `\n`). Whitespace itself is NOT consumed (lookbehind/lookahead are zero-width); only the delimiter run is replaced. The matched run becomes a stashed LITERAL TEXT node, so those delimiter characters are permanently invisible to em_strong / em_strong2. The alternation tries 3, then 2, then 1 asterisks (resp. underscores); a run of 4+ identical delimiters can never satisfy (b) for any of 3/2/1, so 4+ runs are NOT protected.

em_strong PASS (asterisks, priority 60). Trigger regex `\*` (any single asterisk). At each candidate asterisk position p, try these five regexes ANCHORED at p (Python `regex.match(text, p)` semantics: the match must begin exactly at p but may run to any length), in this exact order; the FIRST one that matches wins and its full match span [m.start(0), m.end(0)) is consumed:
  1. EM_STRONG_RE   = `(\*)\1{2}(.+?)\1(.*?)\1{2}`               builder=double , tags=(strong,em)
  2. STRONG_EM_RE   = `(\*)\1{2}(.+?)\1{2}(.*?)\1`               builder=double , tags=(em,strong)
  3. STRONG_EM3_RE  = `(\*)\1(?!\1)([^*]+?)\1(?!\1)(.+?)\1{3}`  builder=double2, tags=(strong,em)
  4. STRONG_RE      = `(\*{2})(.+?)\1`                           builder=single , tags=(strong)
  5. EMPHASIS_RE    = `(\*)([^\*]+)\1`                           builder=single , tags=(em)
All five are compiled with re.DOTALL|re.UNICODE (so `.` matches `\n`; no MULTILINE). If none matches at p, no asterisk emphasis starts at p and the scan moves to the next asterisk. Note there are NO word-boundary or whitespace guards at all on the asterisk patterns — only not_strong (rule above) prevents space-surrounded asterisks from opening emphasis.

em_strong2 PASS (underscores, priority 50). Trigger regex `_`. Same five-slot structure, tried anchored at each underscore position, first match wins:
  1. EM_STRONG2_RE      = `(_)\1{2}(.+?)\1(.*?)\1{2}`                                              builder=double , tags=(strong,em)
  2. STRONG_EM2_RE      = `(_)\1{2}(.+?)\1{2}(.*?)\1`                                              builder=double , tags=(em,strong)
  3. SMART_STRONG_EM_RE = `(?<!\w)(\_)\1(?!\1)(.+?)(?<!\w)\1(?!\1)(.+?)\1{3}(?!\w)`              builder=double2, tags=(strong,em)
  4. SMART_STRONG_RE    = `(?<!\w)(_{2})(?!_)(.+?)(?<!_)\1(?!\w)`                                  builder=single , tags=(strong)
  5. SMART_EMPHASIS_RE  = `(?<!\w)(_)(?!_)(.+?)(?<!_)\1(?!\w)`                                     builder=single , tags=(em)
Flags re.DOTALL|re.UNICODE. CRITICAL ASYMMETRY: slots 1 and 2 (the triple-underscore forms) carry NO word-boundary guards, so they fire intra-word; slots 3, 4 and 5 do carry guards, so `_x_` and `__x__` are 'smart' (word-boundary sensitive) while `___x___` is not.

SMART UNDERSCORE GUARDS IN DETAIL (slots 4 and 5). For `_..._` (slot 5): the opening `_` must not be immediately preceded by a `\w` char (`(?<!\w)`; start-of-text satisfies this), must not be immediately followed by another `_` (`(?!_)`), the body is lazy `(.+?)` (>=1 char, may include newlines), the char immediately before the closing `_` must not be `_` (`(?<!_)`), and the char immediately after the closing `_` must not be a `\w` char (`(?!\w)`; end-of-text satisfies this). Slot 4 is identical with `__` in place of `_`. Because `_` itself IS a `\w` char, `(?<!\w)` also forbids an immediately-preceding underscore. Backtracking applies: if the first candidate closing `_` fails a guard, the lazy body grows and the next `_` is tried.

`\w` DEFINITION (needed for the smart underscore guards). Python `re` with re.UNICODE: `\w` matches a character c iff `c.isalnum()` or c == '_'. Exhaustive enumeration over all of Unicode gives exactly the categories {Lu, Ll, Lt, Lm, Lo, Nd, Nl, No} plus U+005F (the only Pc char included). It does NOT include combining marks (Mn/Mc), punctuation (other than `_`), symbols, or whitespace. JS equivalent: /[\p{L}\p{Nd}\p{Nl}\p{No}_]/u  (equivalently /[\p{L}\p{N}_]/u).

`\s` DEFINITION (needed for not_strong). Python `re` with re.UNICODE: `\s` matches exactly this set of code points: U+0009, U+000A, U+000B, U+000C, U+000D, U+001C, U+001D, U+001E, U+001F, U+0020, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000..U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000. (Identical to `str.isspace()`.) Note U+00A0 NBSP counts as whitespace here, so an NBSP-surrounded `*`/`**`/`***` is neutralised by not_strong.

BUILDER `single` (slots 4,5 of each list). Create element <tag>; take m.group(2) (the body) and run parse_sub_patterns(body, parent=<tag>, last=None, idx=<slot index of the winning pattern>). Result element replaces the whole match.

BUILDER `double` (slots 1,2 of each list; tags='tag1,tag2'). el1=; el2=; parse_sub_patterns(m.group(2), parent=el2, last=None, idx); el1.append(el2); then parse_sub_patterns(m.group(3), parent=el1, last=el2, idx) — i.e. group(3)'s leading plain text becomes el2's TAIL and any elements it produces are appended to el1 AFTER el2. Slot 1 gives (strong,em) => `group2group3`; slot 2 gives (em,strong) => `group2group3`.

BUILDER `double2` (slot 3 of each list; tags='strong,em'). el1=; el2=; parse_sub_patterns(m.group(2), parent=el1, last=None, idx) → group2 becomes el1's TEXT; el1.append(el2); parse_sub_patterns(m.group(3), parent=el2, last=None, idx) → group3 becomes el2's text. Result: `group2group3`.

parse_sub_patterns(data, parent, last, idx) — NESTING INSIDE A MATCHED SPAN. Exact algorithm:
  offset=0; pos=0
  while pos < len(data):
    if the pass's TRIGGER regex matches at pos:
      matched=False
      for index, item in enumerate(PATTERNS):        # 0..4, in list order
        if index <= idx: continue                   # ONLY patterns strictly after the winning parent slot
        m = item.regex.match(data, pos)
        if m:
          text = data[offset:m.start(0)]
          if text: (last.tail = text) if last is not None else (parent.text = text)
          el = build_element(m, item.builder, item.tags, index)
          parent.append(el); last = el
          offset = pos = m.end(0); matched = True
        # NOTE: the for-loop is NOT broken on success; it continues with the NEXT index at the NEW pos
      if not matched: pos += 1
    else: pos += 1
  text = data[offset:]
  if text: (last.tail = text) if last is not None else (parent.text = text)
Key consequences: (a) a span matched by slot 4 can only nest slot-5 constructs; a span matched by slot 5 can nest NOTHING of its own delimiter type; (b) after a nested match, only strictly-higher slot indices are still eligible in that same while-iteration.

CROSS-DELIMITER NESTING (why `_` works inside `*` and vice versa). Immediately after any inline pattern at registry position k produces an ELEMENT node, the tree processor re-runs the REMAINING inline patterns (registry positions k+1 onward, restarting at text index 0 for each) on: node.text, node.tail, and the .text and .tail of each DIRECT child of node — i.e. the iterable `[node] + list(node)`, one level of children only. This step is skipped entirely if node.text is an AtomicString (which is what code spans produce). Because em_strong (60) precedes em_strong2 (50), underscore emphasis is found inside asterisk emphasis; because em_strong2 is last in the registry, nothing is re-scanned inside underscore emphasis.

GREEDY vs LAZY BODIES matter for outcome. EMPHASIS_RE's body is GREEDY `([^\*]+)` — it swallows as many non-asterisk chars as possible, so it always closes on the LAST asterisk reachable without crossing another asterisk. STRONG_RE's body is LAZY `(.+?)` — it closes on the FIRST `**` found. All `(.+?)`/`(.*?)` groups are lazy; `([^*]+?)` in STRONG_EM3_RE is lazy but cannot cross an asterisk. `(.*?)` may match the empty string, `(.+?)` may not.

RUNS OF 4, 5, 6 DELIMITERS. These follow mechanically from slot 1 (EM_STRONG_RE / EM_STRONG2_RE) matching at the first delimiter with the surplus delimiters absorbed into group(2)/group(3) or left as trailing literal text. `****x****` -> group2='*x', group3='' , 8 of 8 chars consumed, one trailing `*` literal. `*****x*****` -> group2='*', group3='x', 8 of 11 consumed, 3 trailing literal. `******x******` -> group2='*', group3='*x', 9 of 13 consumed, 4 trailing literal. Underscores behave identically (slots 1/2 have no word guards).

ASYMMETRIC / UNMATCHED RUNS. No pattern matches => the delimiters stay literal. Because the trigger scan advances one asterisk at a time and each pattern is anchored at the trigger, a failing leading run simply leaves those characters as text and the scan retries at the next asterisk. `**x*`: at p=0 nothing matches (EMPHASIS_RE needs a non-`*` first body char, STRONG_RE needs a second `**`), at p=1 EMPHASIS_RE matches `*x*`. `*x**`: EMPHASIS_RE matches `*x*` at p=0, leaving one literal `*`.

MULTI-LINE SPANS. All emphasis regexes use re.DOTALL, and the paragraph text handed to the inline pass is the block's lines joined with `
` (no trailing newline). Therefore `.` and `[^\*]`/`[^*]` match `
`, and an emphasis span may open on one line and close on a later line of the same paragraph. Since `
` is a `\s` char and a non-`\w` char, a `
` immediately before/after a delimiter satisfies not_strong's `(?<=\s)`/`(?=\s)` and satisfies the smart-underscore `(?<!\w)`/`(?!\w)` guards. `^` and `$` are NOT multiline: `^` only matches text index 0 and `$` only end-of-text.

ESCAPE INTERACTION. The `escape` pattern (priority 180, regex `\\(.)`) runs long before emphasis. If the escaped char is one of ESCAPED_CHARS = ['\\','`','*','_','{','}','[',']','(',')','>','#','+','-','.','!'] the two-char sequence is replaced in the text by `<ord(char)>` (e.g. `\*` -> "42", `\_` -> "95"). That means the delimiter character is GONE from the text seen by not_strong/em_strong/em_strong2, and it is restored to the literal character by the final UnescapeTreeprocessor. Note the substitute's bounding chars are STX/ETX, which are non-`\w` and non-`\s`.

CODE SPAN INTERACTION. The `backtick` pattern (priority 190) runs first, so `*`/`_` inside a code span are already inside a stashed <code> element (whose text is an AtomicString) and are invisible to the emphasis passes; conversely the placeholder left behind is transparent to emphasis bodies and to the `\w` guards (its edges are STX/ETX).

SPACES ADJACENT TO DELIMITERS ARE NOT THEMSELVES A BARRIER for asterisks — only not_strong is. `*x *` and `* x*` do NOT emphasise only because the space-adjacent lone asterisk is neutralised by not_strong (or because the line became a list item); `*a * b*` DOES emphasise across an interior space-surrounded asterisk (that asterisk was neutralised into a literal placeholder that `[^\*]+` can cross). For underscores, in addition to not_strong the smart guards apply, but a space is a non-`\w` char so `_ x _` is neutralised only by not_strong, and `_a b_` emphasises normally.

CONTEXT INDEPENDENCE. The emphasis passes are part of the single inline treeprocessor, so identical rules apply inside headings, list items, blockquotes and link text; there is no context-sensitive variation.

BLOCK-LEVEL PREEMPTION (boundary note, not an emphasis rule). Some delimiter-only lines never reach the inline pass: a line of 3+ `*`, `_` or `-` (optionally space-separated) becomes <hr />, and a line starting `* ` / `- ` / `+ ` becomes a list item. `***` -> <hr />, `** **` -> <hr />, `* x *` -> a <ul> whose item text is `x *`. `_ _` is NOT an hr (needs 3+) and stays a paragraph.

uncertainties: The one-level recursion scope `[node] + list(node)` (rule: 'CROSS-DELIMITER NESTING') is read directly from the bundled treeprocessors bytecode, but I could NOT construct any input over {*, _, a, b} up to length 11 that distinguishes it from full-depth recursion over all descendants. So the depth-1 restriction is source-verified but not behaviourally verified for this area; an implementer who recurses over all descendants will most likely produce identical output for pure-emphasis inputs (it could differ once links/HTML/code are nested 3+ deep inside emphasis).

In `__applyPattern`, when handleMatch returns (None, None, None) the code does `startIndex += match.end(0)` before `continue`. So the accumulation is dead code for emphasis. `build_double` guards the group(3) step with `if len(m.groups()) == 3`. All four `double` patterns have exactly 3 groups, so the guard is always true in practice. Untested for any pattern with a different group count (none exist in the default build).

Exact `\w` membership was determined by enumerating all 0x110000 code points with the local CPython 3.12 `re` module (same interpreter version as the bundle: libpython3.12), giving categories {Lu,Ll,Lt,Lm,Lo,Nd,Nl,No} plus U+005F. rules.rule:
EVIDENCE CONVENTION: every `input` below is an isolated document D, probed as `test14_executable --a $' 'D`; the `output` is the verbatim HTML for `markdown(D)` (i.e. html1 with the leading `

Section 1

` line removed). Blocks are independent, so this equals `markdown(D)` byte-for-byte. Output never ends with a newline.

Inline link: the pattern is `(?<!\!)\[`. On finding a `[` not preceded by `!`, scan forward for the matching `]` counting nested `[`/`]` (depth starts at 1; `[` increments, `]` decrements; the `]` that brings depth to 0 ends the text). If no such `]` exists, the pattern does not match. The link text is the raw substring between the brackets and MAY contain unescaped `[`/`]` pairs.

After the closing `]` the very next character must be `(` (no whitespace allowed between `]` and `(`), otherwise it is not an inline link. Whitespace/newlines immediately AFTER the `(` are allowed and skipped.

Angle-bracket URL form: immediately after `(` plus optional whitespace, try to match `<[^<>]*>` followed by optional whitespace, optionally followed by a quoted title `(['"])(.*?)\1` plus optional whitespace, then `)`. If the whole thing matches: href = the text inside `<>` with leading/trailing whitespace stripped; title = the quoted content (or absent). If the match fails (e.g. text after `>` that is not a quoted title), fall through to the plain scanner, in which case `<` and `>` become literal characters of the href.

Plain (non-angle) URL/title scanner. Let `data` be the whole inline string being scanned and `S` the index just after the `(` and after any whitespace the `\(\s*` prefix consumed. State: bracketCount=1, backtrackCount=1, quote=None, startQuote=-1, exitQuote=-1, altQuote=None, startAlt=-1, exitAlt=-1, last='' , lastBracket=-1, ignore=False. For each position pos from S to end of data with c = data[pos]: (a) if c=='(' : if not ignore then bracketCount+=1 else backtrackCount+=1. (b) if c==')' : if (exitQuote!=-1 and last==quote) or (exitAlt!=-1 and last==altQuote) then bracketCount=0 (TITLE RESOLVED); elif not ignore then bracketCount-=1; else { backtrackCount-=1; if backtrackCount==0 then lastBracket=pos }. (c) if c is `"` or `'`: if quote is None then {quote=c; startQuote=pos; ignore=True; backtrackCount=bracketCount}; elif c==quote then {exitQuote=pos; ignore=False}; elif altQuote is None then {altQuote=c; startAlt=pos}; elif c==altQuote then {exitAlt=pos; ignore=False}. (d) if c!=' ' then last=c  (NOTE: only U+0020 is skipped; a newline DOES update `last`). (e) if bracketCount==0 break. On break: if TITLE RESOLVED via quote -> href=data[S:startQuote], title=data[startQuote+1:exitQuote]; if via altQuote -> href=data[S:startAlt], title=data[startAlt+1:exitAlt]; else href=data[S:pos], title=None. Link consumes through pos (next scan index = pos+1). href is then `.strip()`ed; title has every whitespace character replaced by a single space.

A title is only recognized when a `)` is reached whose last preceding non-space character is the closing quote. A newline between the closing quote and the `)` therefore kills the title (newline updates `last`), while any number of plain spaces does not. Tabs never reach this stage because the whitespace preprocessor expands them to spaces (tab stop 4).

Fallback A: if the scan ends (end of data) with bracketCount != 0 but lastBracket != -1, the link is accepted with pos = lastBracket: href = data[S:lastBracket].strip(), title = None, next scan index = lastBracket+1. lastBracket is the `)` at which backtrackCount (initialised to the bracket depth in effect when the first quote opened) reaches 0.

Fallback B (QUIRK): if a `(` is encountered while `ignore` is True (i.e. after an opened quote whose title never resolves), the link is still accepted but its end is forced to len(data)-1, i.e. href = data[S : len(data)-2].strip() and the next scan index is len(data)-1, so exactly the LAST character of the inline string being scanned is left as the link's tail. This happens even when there is no closing `)` at all.
If the scan reaches end of data with bracketCount != 0 and lastBracket == -1 (no quote was ever opened, so nothing to backtrack to), the construct is not a link and is emitted literally.

An `` element always gets `href` (possibly the empty string). `title` is emitted whenever a quoted title was found, including when it is empty. Attributes are serialised in lexicographic order (`href` before `title`; for ``: `alt`, `src`, `title`).

Attribute-value escaping in the serializer: `&` -> `&` ONLY when it is not already the start of `&#<digits>;`, `&#x<hexdigits>;` or `&<alphanumerics>;` (any alphanumeric run, valid entity or not); `<` -> `<`; `>` -> `>`; `"` -> `"`. Single quotes and newlines are NOT escaped.
No URL sanitising, percent-encoding or normalisation is performed: `javascript:` URLs, spaces, and raw parens all pass through as-is (only escaped/entity handling and attribute escaping apply).

Backslash escapes are resolved BEFORE link parsing (escape pattern has higher priority). `\X` is an escape only when X is one of `\ ` ` * _ { } [ ] ( ) > # + - . !`; the escaped character is hidden from the link scanner (so `\]`, `\)`, `\(` do not affect bracket/paren counting) and reappears literally in href/title/text. `\` before any other character (including `"` and space) stays literal.

Title whitespace normalisation: every single whitespace character in the title is replaced by one space (per-character, not collapsing runs). The href is only `.strip()`ed; internal whitespace, including newlines, is preserved verbatim.

Images: pattern `!\[`, then the same balanced-bracket text scan and the same URL/title scanner as links. Produces `` with `src`, optional `title`, and `alt`. `alt` is the raw link text with inline placeholders replaced by their PLAIN TEXT content only (tags stripped) — because backtick code spans and links/images are processed before the image pattern, their markup is removed from alt, while emphasis/raw-HTML/entities (processed later) stay literal in alt.

Inline-pattern precedence (higher runs first): backtick 190, escape 180, reference 170, link 160, image_link 150, image_reference 140, short_reference 130, short_image_ref 125, autolink 120, automail 110, linebreak 100, raw-html 90, entity 80, em/strong 70..50. A pattern's produced element has its TEXT re-scanned only with patterns of LOWER priority than the current one; consequently a link inside link text is normally left literal, but an IMAGE or an AUTOLINK inside link text IS converted.

QUIRK (nested-link resurrection): after placeholders are resolved, every produced element is pushed back on the tree-walk stack, and the TAILS of its child elements are re-scanned with ALL patterns from priority 0. So a `[a](u)` that sits in the tail of a child element inside link text DOES become a nested `<a>`, whereas the same text sitting in the parent's own `.text` does not.

URL autolink: `<((?:[Ff]|[Hh][Tt])[Tt][Pp][Ss]?://[^<>]*)>` — i.e. only the schemes http, https, ftp, ftps, case-insensitive, and the `://` is mandatory. href and text are both the captured string verbatim (spaces and `*`/`_` allowed); the text is atomic, so no further inline processing happens inside it.
Bare URLs are never auto-linked (no `http://x.com` -> link, no `www.` linking).

Email autolink: `<([^<> !]+@[^@<> ]+)>` (local part may contain anything but `<`, `>`, space and `!`, including newline, quotes and `/`; domain part additionally excludes `@`). A leading lowercase `mailto:` is stripped from the address (uppercase `MAILTO:` is not). Output is fully deterministic: href = each character of `"mailto:" + address` encoded as a DECIMAL numeric character reference `&#N;`; the link TEXT = each character of the address encoded as its HTML4 NAMED entity when `html.entities.codepoint2name` has one, otherwise `&#N;`.

Angle-bracket text that is neither an autolink nor an email is passed through as RAW HTML (verbatim, unescaped) when it matches the inline raw-HTML pattern `<(/?[a-zA-Z][^<>]*|!--…--)>` AND the first whitespace-delimited token (the tag-name part after the optional `/`) contains no `@`. Otherwise the `<`/`>` remain literal text and are escaped to `<`/`>`, and inline markup inside is still processed.

Reference definition (a block processor, tried on every block before all other block processors): regex, with re.MULTILINE, `^[ ]{0,3}\[([^\[\]]*)\]:[ ]*\n?[ ]*<?([^\s>]+)>?[ ]*(?:\n?[ ]*((?<=\s)['"](.*)['"]|\((.*)\))[ ]*)?$`, applied with `search` (not `match`). The FIRST match anywhere in the block is removed; text before it and text after it are pushed back as separate blocks. id = group1.strip().lower(); url = group2 with one optional surrounding `<`…`>` removed; title = the inner text of the `"…"`/`'…'`/`(…)` group. A 4-space-indented line is a code block instead. Nothing is emitted for the definition itself.

Definition continuation lines: the URL may be on the line after `[id]:`, and the title on the line after the URL (at most one newline before each, plus any spaces). A title may NOT span lines. Multiple definitions in one block all register (the leftover block is re-processed).

All block parsing (hence all definition collection) finishes before inline processing, so a definition may appear anywhere in the document — before or after its use, and inside a blockquote or list item (leaving the container empty).

Full reference link `[text][id]`: after the balanced-bracket text scan, match `\s?\[([^\]]*)\]` — i.e. AT MOST ONE whitespace character (space or newline) between `]` and `[`. The raw id is lower-cased, then every run of whitespace in it is collapsed to one space; it is NOT stripped. If empty, the id is the lower-cased link text. If the id is not in the reference table the pattern does not produce a node and scanning resumes just after it (so a later reference on the same line still works).

Shortcut reference `[text]` (and `![text]`): id = lower-cased link text with whitespace runs collapsed to one space; matches only if defined. Also works for images via `![id]` / `![text][id]` / `![text][]`. Empty brackets `[]` / `[][]` never match.

Line break: the inline pattern is exactly two spaces followed by a newline (` \n`), matched leftmost-first, and it CONSUMES all three characters, producing an empty `
` element. Because it is leftmost, with N>=2 trailing spaces the first N-2 spaces survive in the text. One trailing space (or a tab that expands to fewer than 2 columns of padding) produces no `
`. A trailing backslash never produces a break.

A prettify tree-processor then rewrites the tail of EVERY `
` element: if the tail is empty or whitespace-only it becomes exactly "\n"; otherwise it becomes "\n" + the original tail. Hence `
` is always immediately followed by a newline, and leading whitespace on the following line is DELETED when nothing else precedes the next child element, but PRESERVED when the tail contains non-whitespace.

Trailing spaces on the LAST line of a block never produce `
` (there is no following newline inside the block) and are preserved verbatim in the output text. A line consisting only of spaces is emptied by the whitespace preprocessor, so it terminates the paragraph instead of creating a break.

`
` works inside link text, blockquotes and other inline contexts; it is not produced inside an image `alt` (the two spaces and the newline stay literal there, because the image pattern runs before the linebreak pattern) and headings strip trailing whitespace before inline processing.
Link text may be empty; unmatched trailing `]` or `)` are left as literal text; two adjacent links/images produce adjacent elements with no separator inserted.

uncertainties: Fallback B (the `len(data)-2` quirk) is derived purely empirically from 10 probes and is stated in terms of `len(data)`, where `data` is the string currently being scanned by the inline engine. For a top-level paragraph that string is the paragraph's text after `lstrip()`. I did NOT verify what `len(data)` means when the same construct appears inside link text, a heading, a list item, or after other inline placeholders have already been substituted into the string (placeholders are ~10 characters long and would change `len(data)`). An implementer must re-probe those contexts. The `@`-in-tag-name exclusion for inline raw HTML is an observed fact I could not map to a source regex. I verified: `@` anywhere in the first whitespace-delimited token (after the optional leading `/`) prevents raw-HTML passthrough (`<a@b c>`, `<a@>`, `<a=b@c d>`, `</a@b c>` all escape), while `@` after the first space is fine (`<a b@c>`, `<a b @c>`, `<a b@c d>` all pass through raw). I did not determine whether `ignore` is also cleared when the SECONDARY (alt) quote closes (`exitAlt`), only that it is cleared when the primary quote closes. Construct a probe like `[t](u 'a "b" (c) d)` to settle it if needed.

The exact slice used for the alt-quote title (`data[startAlt+1:exitAlt]`) was confirmed by only one probe (`A[t](u 'a "b" )B` -> href `u 'a`, title `b`). Multi-alt-quote cases (three or more `"` inside a `'…'` region) were not probed.
Whether `title` is emitted when the reference-definition title group is present but empty (e.g. `[id]: u ""`) was not probed; for inline links an empty quoted title IS emitted (`title=""`).
The reference table is per-`markdown()` call, so definitions do not leak between the four separate `markdown()` invocations in the harness — assumed, not probed.
I did not probe reference definitions inside deeply nested containers (list inside blockquote), nor definitions whose id contains a newline (`[a\nb]: u`).

Unicode/IDN URLs, surrogate pairs, and characters above U+00FF in email addresses were not probed (only é U+00E9, £ U+00A3, × U+00D7, © U+00A9, all of which map to HTML4 named entities in the link text).

result.area: Unicode / CJK / mixed-script behavior + stress & adversarial inputs (Python-Markdown 3.10.2, no extensions)

rules.rule: Output is raw UTF-8. Non-ASCII characters (CJK, full-width punctuation, emoji, RTL, combining marks) are NEVER escaped, entity-encoded, percent-encoded, or Unicode-normalized. They pass through byte-identically in paragraph text, headers, list items, blockquotes, code spans, code blocks, link text, link hrefs and titles, and HTML attributes. Only `&`, `<`, `>` are escaped (and `"` inside attribute values). Implementation note: do NOT call String.prototype.normalize() anywhere.

WORD-CHARACTER CLASS (`\w`) — the single most important Unicode decision. Python's `\w` is used for the smart-underscore-emphasis lookarounds. Define isWord(cp) = (Unicode general category of cp is one of Lu, Ll, Lt, Lm, Lo, Nd, Nl, No) OR cp === 0x5F ('_'). Equivalently: `Py_UNICODE_ISALNUM(cp) || cp === '_'`, i.e. Python's `str.isalnum()`. Consequences: ALL CJK ideographs, Hiragana/Katakana, Hangul, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, full-width Latin letters AND full-width digits, U+3005 々 (Lm), U+3006 〆 (Lo), U+3007 〇 (Nl), U+30FC ー (Lm), U+00B9 ¹ (No), U+2177 ⅷ (Nl) ARE word characters. NOT word characters: emoji and all So/Sm/Sc/Sk symbols (😀 🀄 ☃ ± § ¥ = +), all combining marks Mn/Mc (U+0301, U+3099, U+0E31, U+FE0F VS16), all format chars Cf (U+200E LRM, U+200F RLM, U+200B ZWSP, U+FEFF, U+200D ZWJ), all Zs/whitespace, U+30FB ・ (Po). CRITICAL for JS: this must be evaluated per CODE POINT, not per UTF-16 unit — astral-plane letters (U+1D400 𝐀 Lu, U+2000B 𠀋 Lo, U+104B0 𐒰 Lu, U+1D7D9 𝟙 Nd) ARE word chars, while astral symbols (U+1F004 🀄 So) are not. JS `\w` is ASCII-only and is NOT a substitute; a `[\p{L}\p{Nd}\p{Nl}\p{No}_]` /u class is the correct equivalent.

SMART UNDERSCORE EMPHASIS pattern is exactly `(?<!\w)(_)(?!_)(.+?)(?<!_)\1(?!\w)` (and strong: `(?<!\w)(__)(?!_)(.+?)(?<!_)\1(?!\w)`), with `\w` per the rule above and LAZY `.+?` that BACKTRACKS/expands until the trailing `(?!\w)` is satisfied. So `_中_文_字_` matches with content `中_文_字` (the parser tries `中`, fails `(?!\w)` on 文; tries `中_文`, fails on 字; then `中_文_字` succeeds at end-of-string). `中文_下_线` fails on BOTH lookarounds (leading 文 is \w, trailing 线 is \w) → literal. `中文_下_ 线` still fails only on the leading lookbehind → literal, proving CJK is \w for the lookbehind. `😀_a_ b` succeeds (😀 not \w, space not \w). `😀_a_b` fails only on the trailing `(?!\w)` (b is \w) and no expansion is possible → literal.

ASTERISK emphasis/strong have NO word-boundary rule at all (patterns are `(\*)([^\*]+)\1` for em and `(\*{2})(.+?)\1` for strong). CJK directly adjacent to `*` on either side always works. So `中*文*字` → em, while `中_文_字` → literal. `*中*文*字*` yields `中文字` because the em pattern's content class `[^\*]+` cannot cross an asterisk (contrast with the underscore pattern's `.+?` which can).

This differs from JS in two directions: JS `\s`/`trim()` include U+FEFF (must be excluded) and exclude U+0085 and U+001C-U+001F (must be included). Verified via the NOT_STRONG_RE rule `((^|\s)(\*{1,3}|_{1,3})(?=\s|$))`, which converts a lone asterisk/underscore run surrounded by whitespace into literal text: for every char in the set, `A<c>*<c>B<c>*<c>C` leaves the asterisks literal; for U+FEFF and U+200B it produces `<em>`.

DIGIT CLASS (`\d`) for the ordered-list marker `^[ ]{0,3}\d+\.[ ]+` is Unicode category Nd ONLY (decimal digits), evaluated per code point (astral Nd counts). TAB EXPANSION is `expandtabs(4)` counted in CODE POINTS, not display columns. A CJK ideograph occupies exactly ONE column even though it is double-width visually. `中\tx` → 中 at column 0, tab at column 1, next stop 4 → THREE spaces. `中中中中\tx` → tab at column 4, next stop 8 → FOUR spaces.
